[THOUGHT]  
The clinical picture centers on **acute-to-subacute, isolated right upper limb weakness with objective sensory loss in the same distribution**, but *no other neurological deficits* (intact gait, coordination, cranial nerves, and normal reflexes bilaterally). The discordance between subjective denial of sensory symptoms and objective sensory loss is notable — this pattern is classically seen in **structural lesions affecting both motor and sensory pathways in a focal, anatomically coherent distribution**, rather than functional disorders (which typically show non-anatomic or inconsistent patterns).  

Key localizing clues:  
- Unilateral arm involvement only → rules out diffuse or bilateral processes (e.g., metabolic neuropathy, early ALS, myopathy).  
- Normal reflexes argue *against* a classic corticospinal tract lesion (which usually causes hyperreflexia) and also *against* lower motor neuron disease (which causes hyporeflexia/areflexia). This makes pure motor cortex or spinal cord corticospinal tract lesions less likely.  
- Sensory loss in the same limb strongly suggests involvement of sensory pathways — i.e., dorsal root, dorsal root ganglion, brachial plexus, or cervical cord (dorsal columns or spinothalamic tract).  
- Absence of fasciculations, atrophy, or cramps makes ALS highly unlikely at this stage — and the normal reflexes further undermine that diagnosis.  
- The progressive course over weeks favors a structural or inflammatory process over acute stroke (which would be sudden) or chronic degeneration (which would be insidious over months–years).  
- Brachial plexopathy (e.g., neuralgic amyotrophy or tumor/inflammatory plexitis) fits well: it commonly presents with asymmetric, painful or painless arm weakness + sensory loss, often with preserved reflexes early on, and can have dissociation between subjective and objective sensory findings due to cortical modulation or attention effects.  
- Cervical radiculopathy (e.g., C5–C7 root compression) is plausible, but typically causes *dermatomal* sensory loss and *myotomal* weakness — and reflex changes (e.g., diminished biceps or triceps reflex) are expected if roots are involved. Here, reflexes are *normal*, making isolated single-root compression less likely.  
- Cervical myelopathy (e.g., compressive cord lesion) could cause ipsilateral arm weakness + sensory loss, but usually includes signs below the level (e.g., leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, gait disturbance) — all absent here. So a *purely unilateral, arm-limited* myelopathy is atypical.  
- Brain MRI may rule out cortical/subcortical lesion — but a purely motor cortex lesion wouldn’t explain sensory loss; a lesion involving both precentral gyrus *and* postcentral gyrus would be large and likely cause additional deficits (e.g., facial involvement, neglect, aphasia if dominant side), none of which are present.  
- Thus, the most parsimonious localization is **right brachial plexus** — particularly the *upper trunk* (C5–C6), which supplies shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, and sensation over lateral arm/deltoid and lateral forearm. Strength 2/5 in the entire right arm fits upper trunk involvement (though severe), and sensory loss in the arm aligns. Normal reflexes are consistent with early or incomplete plexopathy — EMG/NCS will be decisive.  

[EVIDENCE]  
- Progressive right upper limb weakness over weeks, now functionally impairing  
- Objective decreased sensation in right arm (despite patient’s denial)  
- Right arm strength 2/5; left arm 5/5  
- No other motor deficits (no gait/balance issues, no facial/arm/leg weakness elsewhere)  
- Normal reflexes bilaterally (biceps, triceps, brachioradialis)  
- Intact coordination  
- No fasciculations, cramps, or atrophy observed or reported  
- Normal CBC (rules out systemic inflammation or hematologic malignancy as obvious driver)  
- No headache, visual changes, dysarthria, or cognitive complaints  

[GAPS]  
- EMG/NCS results (critical to confirm plexus vs. root vs. peripheral nerve lesion and assess for acute denervation)  
- MRI cervical spine (to exclude compressive tumor, cyst, or inflammatory mass involving plexus origin or proximal roots)  
- MRI brain (to definitively exclude rare cortical or subcortical lesion with unusual presentation)  
- Serum CK (to assess for occult myositis or neurogenic muscle damage)  
- Inflammatory/autoimmune serologies (e.g., ANA, ESR/CRP, anti-ganglioside antibodies) — not yet ordered, but relevant if plexopathy suspected  

[ESCALATION]  
- Paraneoplastic brachial plexopathy (e.g., from lung cancer): would require identification of an underlying malignancy (e.g., on chest imaging or PET) or positive onconeural antibodies — not yet evaluated.  
- Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy (CIDP) with asymmetric onset: would require CSF protein elevation, nerve conduction slowing/demyelination on NCS, and/or response to immunotherapy — not yet assessed.  
- Cervical spinal cord tumor (e.g., intradural extramedullary meningioma): would require MRI showing enhancing intradural mass compressing ventral and dorsal structures — pending.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Right upper trunk brachial plexopathy.

- Unilateral arm involvement only → rules out diffuse or bilateral processes (e.g., metabolic neuropathy, early ALS, myopathy).  
- Normal reflexes argue *against* a classic corticospinal tract lesion (which usually causes hyperreflexia) and also *against* lower motor neuron disease (which causes hyporeflexia/areflexia). This makes pure motor cortex or spinal cord corticospinal tract lesions less likely.  
- Sensory loss in the same limb strongly suggests involvement of sensory pathways — i.e., dorsal root, dorsal root ganglion, brachial plexus, or cervical cord (dorsal columns or spinothalamic tract).  
- Absence of fasciculations, atrophy, or cramps makes ALS highly unlikely at this stage — and the normal reflexes further undermine that diagnosis.  
- The progressive course over weeks favors a structural or inflammatory process over acute stroke (which would be sudden) or chronic degeneration (which would be insidious over months–years).  
- Brachial plexopathy (e.g., neuralgic amyotrophy or tumor/inflammatory plexitis) fits well: it commonly presents with asymmetric, painful or painless arm weakness + sensory loss, often with preserved reflexes early on, and can have dissociation between subjective and objective sensory findings due to cortical modulation or attention effects.  
- Cervical radiculopathy (e.g., C5–C7 root compression) is plausible, but typically causes *dermatomal* sensory loss and *myotomal* weakness — and reflex changes (e.g., diminished biceps or triceps reflex) are expected if roots are involved. Here, reflexes are *normal*, making isolated single-root compression less likely.  
- Cervical myelopathy (e.g., compressive cord lesion) could cause ipsilateral arm weakness + sensory loss, but usually includes signs below the level (e.g., leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, gait disturbance) — all absent here. So a *purely unilateral, arm-limited* myelopathy is atypical.  
- Brain MRI may rule out cortical/subcortical lesion — but a purely motor cortex lesion wouldn’t explain sensory loss; a lesion involving both precentral gyrus *and* postcentral gyrus would be large and likely cause additional deficits (e.g., facial involvement, neglect, aphasia if dominant side), none of which are present.  
- Thus, the most parsimonious localization is **right brachial plexus** — particularly the *upper trunk* (C5–C6), which supplies shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, and sensation over lateral arm/deltoid and lateral forearm. Strength 2/5 in the entire right arm fits upper trunk involvement (though severe), and sensory loss in the arm aligns. Normal reflexes are consistent with early or incomplete plexopathy — EMG/NCS will be decisive.  

[EVIDENCE]  
- Progressive right upper limb weakness over weeks, now functionally impairing  
- Objective decreased sensation in right arm (despite patient’s denial)  
- Right arm strength 2/5; left arm 5/5  
- No other motor deficits (no gait/balance issues, no facial/arm/leg weakness elsewhere)  
- Normal reflexes bilaterally (biceps, triceps, brachioradialis)  
- Intact coordination  
- No fasciculations, cramps, or atrophy observed or reported  
- Normal CBC (rules out systemic inflammation or hematologic malignancy as obvious driver)  
- No headache, visual changes, dysarthria, or cognitive complaints  

[GAPS]  
- EMG/NCS results (critical to confirm plexus vs. root vs. peripheral nerve lesion and assess for acute denervation)  
- MRI cervical spine (to exclude compressive tumor, cyst, or inflammatory mass involving plexus origin or proximal roots)  
- MRI brain (to definitively exclude rare cortical or subcortical lesion with unusual presentation)  
- Serum CK (to assess for occult myositis or neurogenic muscle damage)  
- Inflammatory/autoimmune serologies (e.g., ANA, ESR/CRP, anti-ganglioside antibodies) — not yet ordered, but relevant if plexopathy suspected  

[ESCALATION]  
- Paraneoplastic brachial plexopathy (e.g., from lung cancer): would require identification of an underlying malignancy (e.g., on chest imaging or PET) or positive onconeural antibodies — not yet evaluated.  
- Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy (CIDP) with asymmetric onset: would require CSF protein elevation, nerve conduction slowing/demyelination on NCS, and/or response to immunotherapy — not yet assessed.  
- Cervical spinal cord tumor (e.g., intradural extramedullary meningioma): would require MRI showing enhancing intradural mass compressing ventral and dorsal structures — pending.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Right upper trunk brachial plexopathy.
